初學可先從單鼓操作開始：傳統約拉鼓手一次只擊一鼓，通常一手持棒、一手拍擊牛皮鼓面: A beginner can start from the single drum: a traditional Jola drummer strikes one drum at a time, usually holding a stick in one hand and slapping the cowhide head with the other. Once in a modern drum set, the player stands and strikes three or four cup-shaped drums with both hands in alternation, producing a low melodic line. The essential thing is to strike the single head and keep the rhythm steady; the metal bracelets the player wears add to the sound. With no tutor to hand, the order of practice can be to get used to the single-drum stroke first and then move both hands around the drum set.

布加拉布鼓常見於西非，尤其塞內加爾南部、卡薩芒斯與岡比亞一帶的約拉社群。傳統場合: The bougarabou is common in West Africa, especially among the Jola communities of southern Senegal, Casamance and the Gambia. On traditional occasions the audience and dancers form a circle, clapping and singing, and usually a single drummer supplies the drumming with three or four drums; the metal bracelets worn by the drummer also take part in the sound. In modern percussion line-ups it is often played with the djembe and tama, producing something like a bass melody within the overall rhythm, and it also appears in groups that add other small Jola drums.
布加拉布鼓是西非常見的一組膜鳴鼓，源自塞內加爾南部、卡薩芒斯與甘比亞的約拉族群。: The bougarabou is a group of membranophone drums common in West Africa, coming from the Jola people of southern Senegal, Casamance and the Gambia. The body is an elongated cup or roughly conical shape, covered on one face with cowhide, usually set on a single stand, most often in a group of three or four drums. Modern playing is mostly by a single drummer standing and using the hands, whereas earlier only one drum was struck at a time, often with a stick in one hand. As the music goes on, the audience and dancers form a circle, clapping and singing, sometimes accompanied by blocks of palm-flower stalk, making an occasion in which the drum group carries the rhythm.
布加拉布鼓源自塞內加爾南部卡薩芒斯與甘比亞一帶的約拉（Jola）族，包括布魯夫、: The bougarabou comes from the Jola (Jola) people of Casamance in southern Senegal and the Gambia, including branches such as the Buluf, Foni and Karonai. At first only one drum was played at a time, usually with a stick in one hand; from the 1940s, possibly under the influence of conga players in the Western Hemisphere, sets of several drums appeared. Unlike many African tribal settings, it is traditionally played by a single drummer standing and using both hands, while the audience and dancers circle, clap and sing; sets of three or four drums are found today as well, played together with the djembe and others.
布加拉布鼓的鼓身採用空心圓錐形木製構件，通常選用非洲本地硬木製作以增強共鳴。鼓面: The body of the bougarabou is a hollow conical wooden piece, usually made from local African hardwood to strengthen the resonance. The head is a single layer of cowhide or another natural animal skin, treated by traditional tanning. The stand is made of wood, designed to carry and hold the body. Traditional bougarabou are made entirely of natural materials, with no metal or synthetic material at all, which keeps the instrument's original character and its warm timbre.
布加拉布鼓音色溫暖深沉，具有明顯的非洲鼓樂特徵。其單層牛皮鼓面能產生豐富的中低音: The bougarabou has a warm, deep timbre with clear features of African drumming. Its single cowhide head produces a rich low and middle register, round in quality and full of resonance. Struck at the centre the sound is low and heavy; struck near the rim it turns brighter, with more high frequency. The conical resonating chamber lets the sound extend naturally, producing a warm harmonic ring. Compared with the sharp sound of the conga, the bougarabou is more restrained and calm; compared with the jazz drum kit it has more of an organic warmth. Its sound carries well, so in a band it delivers the rhythm clearly while keeping the original flavour of traditional African percussion, and it suits a mysterious, strongly rhythmic atmosphere.
